episode_title: E83: Southeast Texas Economic Outlook: 2024–2034 Occupational Projections & Wage Trends

real_qa.q: What are the occupational projections for Southeast Texas from 2024 to 2034, and which occupations show the highest average annual openings?
real_qa.r: According to the 2024-2034 occupational projections for Southeast Texas, occupations with the highest average annual openings include general operations managers, construction laborers, material movers, heavy tractor and trailer truck drivers, welders, electricians, maintenance and repair workers, petroleum pump system operators, and registered nurses. These projections are created by analyzing 10-20 years of industry employment trend data, then applying staffing patterns to translate industry needs into occupational demand. The projections program also estimates average annual openings by accounting for job growth plus backfilling from retirement and occupational transitions.

real_qa.q: What percentage growth is projected for petroleum and coal products manufacturing in Southeast Texas over the next 10 years?
real_qa.r: Petroleum and coal products manufacturing is projected to experience 13.3 percent growth over the next 10 years in Southeast Texas, based on past hiring trends from the previous 10 to 20 years. This growth occurs even as the overall manufacturing sector remains relatively flat, demonstrating that certain subsectors within manufacturing show strong growth potential.
real_qa.requete: petroleum coal products manufacturing Southeast Texas growth 13.3

real_qa.q: How has healthcare employment grown in Southeast Texas, and why is it considered a demand-inelastic industry?
real_qa.r: Healthcare is classified as demand-inelastic because people prioritize healthcare spending even during economic downturns—they may postpone vacations or car purchases but will seek medical care when needed. Additionally, third-party payers like employer health insurance and government programs insulate healthcare demand from business cycles. Combined with an aging population and statewide population growth, healthcare is projected as a significant source of opportunities and growth across Texas regions. Many healthcare occupations, including middle-skilled roles like nursing staff, radiology technicians, and medical billing professionals, provide good wages without requiring a four-year graduate degree or extensive student debt.

real_qa.q: What is the average weekly wage in Southeast Texas for the first quarter of 2026, and how does wage growth compare to the statewide average?
real_qa.r: Average weekly wages for Southeast Texas exceeded $1,400 in the first quarter of 2026. Over the past five years, Southeast Texas average weekly wages have risen by just over 30 percent, which is almost exactly the same as the statewide number. Much of this recent wage growth in Southeast Texas is attributable to the region's recovery from COVID-19's disproportionate impact on construction and manufacturing—industries that cannot be teleworked—which occurred later than in other parts of the state.
real_qa.requete: Southeast Texas average weekly wage 2026 first quarter

real_qa.q: How much job openings growth is expected in professional business services and professional scientific and technical services in Southeast Texas?
real_qa.r: Professional business services are projected to grow by approximately 9.4 percent over 10 years, while professional scientific and technical services—which include accounting firms, engineering consulting firms, and IT services—are projected to grow by about 9.9 percent. This growth reflects a broader decades-long shift toward a more service-based economy occurring nationally, with professional scientific and technical consulting services showing particularly strong percentage growth within that sector.

transcript_full: Welcome to Southeast Texas Works, the official podcast of Workforce Solutions of Southeast Texas. And now here's your host, Kevin King. That's probably what most people associate with labor market data. But there's actually a lot more data out there on people who are working. And actually, I think that's more of an interesting part of the story. So what we basically do is we help people understand their local economy. It's becoming a more challenging labor market, certainly in the U.S., but probably worldwide. And the rest of Texas is not exempt from that. So the big picture is that the labor market is going to be more challenging anywhere. simply because that's the world we're in right now. And Southeast Texas is not going to be exempt from that. So I would say that Southeast Texas, it may be a challenging time for some people who are going into the labor market. So if you are training for things that employers need, there is still a lot of opportunities to have a good labor market outcome. It's just going to require a lot more work. So just to clarify, when we say Southeast Texas WDA, we're talking about Jefferson, Orange and Hardin counties. Those are the three counties that are part of our area here in Southeast Texas. One of the things that is important to know is that we are entering an inflationary period in the economy. Again, that's a national trend. In terms of Southeast Texas, the average weekly wage over the last five years in Southeast Texas has gone up a little over 30 percent, which is almost exactly the same as the analogous statewide number. So over the last five years, the numbers are fairly similar to what you see statewide. Those were activities that could not be teleworked. So some of the rapid recovery that you saw from COVID that occurred in other places in, say, 22 and 23 occurred in 24 in Southeast Texas. 24 was a very, very good year for Southeast Texas in terms of job growth and a lot of other metrics. So when we look at occupational projections, can you kind of give a little background on how do you guys come up with your occupational projections? I believe the latest ones that were released were from 2024 to 2034. Is that correct? Can you kind of give a little background on that? Yes. What we do is we have a projections program every other year. We take a look at the industry, the industry employment. employment going back the last 10 or 20 years and say, if this trend line continues, where will this industry be 10 years from our base year? That's based on our quarterly census of employment and wages, which is pulled from unemployment tax records and supplemented by additional information we collect from employers. So we look at that industry trend line and then we take what we call staffing patterns. And a staffing pattern is like a translator between industries, which are what the company does, and occupations, which is what the person does. And so it will tell you, okay, in this industry, what occupations do they hire? So what occupations do manufacturing employers hire? Do leisure and hospitality employers hire? And we then use that industry projection to create, based on the staffing patterns, our occupational projections. And our occupational projections give us an idea of what professions might be in demand in the next 10 years, what demand looks like. But we go one step further. We also produce a number called average annual openings. Because one thing that's important for people to understand about the labor market, and this could be very important, especially in Southeast Texas, there are three ways a job can become open. And what the projections program does is it uses national research on occupational turnover because some occupations turn over faster than others in terms of have vacancies. And it estimates the three components of openings, because growth alone doesn't tell you how much of an occupation you're going to need. You also have to look at backfilling for people who move to another occupation or who retire or for one reason or another can no longer be in that job. So that's what our projections program does.
